What Four Years of Remote-Work Data Actually Tell Us

By Jordan Mehta · March 14, 2024

Four years on from the pandemic-era shift to working from home, the data on remote and hybrid work has finally caught up with the rhetoric. The picture is messier than either side of the debate would have you believe — but it is no longer ambiguous.

The most cited piece of evidence is a 2022 study by Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom and colleagues, which found that hybrid work arrangements increased worker productivity by 4.4 percent compared to fully in-office controls. The study followed 1,612 engineers, marketing staff, and finance employees at a large Chinese travel company over six months and is widely considered the largest randomized trial of hybrid work to date.

Government data tells a complementary story. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 27 percent of U.S. employees worked from home at least one day per week in 2023, more than five times the pre-pandemic share. The trend appears to have stabilized rather than reversed, despite high-profile return-to-office mandates from companies like Amazon and JPMorgan.

Bloom himself, in a recent interview, was direct about the implications. “We’ve collected enough data now to say hybrid is here to stay,” he told the Financial Times. “The argument is no longer whether it works — it does — but how to manage it well.”

Workers themselves report similar effects. Microsoft’s 2023 Work Trend Index, a survey of 31,000 workers across 31 countries, found that 64 percent of respondents said workplace flexibility had improved their work-life balance. Critics, however, argue these gains may erode over time as companies recalibrate.

Not everyone is convinced. In a now-famous 2021 remark, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon called working from home “an aberration that we’re going to correct as soon as possible.” Three years later, Goldman remains one of the strictest enforcers of full in-office attendance among major Wall Street firms.

The truth, most likely, lies in the dull middle: hybrid work modestly improves productivity for knowledge workers, modestly improves retention, and modestly complicates middle management. None of this is the revolution its loudest advocates promised. None of it is the catastrophe its critics warned of either.
